title: Is the U.S. Banking System Ready for a Post-Quantum Future?
gist: CSIS's Sultan Meghji argues US bank regulators must set a post-quantum cryptography migration deadline (aligned to the federal 2030-2031 clock) because 'harvest now, decrypt later' collection by China and Russia is already underway, disclosure is incoherent across ~8,500 institutions, and SWIFT is effectively setting the timetable; supervising core processors FIS, Fiserv and Jack Henry could fix thousands of banks at once.

insights.claim: Federal high-value systems are on a 2030-2031 post-quantum migration clock under Executive Order 14412 and OMB Memorandum M-26-15, yet no US banking regulator (Federal Reserve, OCC or others) has set a deadline for the banks they supervise.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A supervisory deadline would trigger a multiyear bank cybersecurity spending wave; watch Treasury/FFIEC actions.
insights.quote: The federal government has imposed a deadline on itself while leaving the financial system largely to an advisory timetable.

insights.claim: The G7 Cyber Expert Group, cochaired by the US Treasury and Bank of England, set a financial-sector roadmap in January calling for critical systems to transition by 2030-2032 and full migration by 2035.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Provides the likely benchmark dates regulators will eventually adopt.
insights.locator: In January, the G7 Cyber Expert Group

insights.claim: SWIFT has set a mandatory Release 8.0 for end-July 2027 on a path to post-quantum readiness, with Release 7.9 losing support 15 months later, so a Belgian cooperative is imposing an operational migration clock on US banks before any US regulator.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Real forcing deadline for bank IT spend is 2027-2028 via SWIFT, not US regulation.
insights.quote: A Belgian cooperative is therefore imposing an operational migration clock on U.S. institutions before any U.S. regulator has set a comparable date.

insights.claim: Shor's algorithm on a capable quantum computer would break public-key cryptography by making factoring and discrete-log problems tractable; symmetric encryption degrades but survives.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Focus remediation (and vendor opportunity) on public-key infrastructure: certificates, HSMs, protocols.
insights.locator: What the Threat Is, and What Fixing It Takes

insights.claim: Adversaries including China and Russia are already collecting encrypted financial traffic to decrypt later, per former deputy national security adviser Anne Neuberger; harvested traffic cannot be protected retroactively and any record needing confidentiality past 2030 is already exposed.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Every month of delay increases exposure; urgency argues for accelerated PQC spending.
insights.quote: Any record that must remain confidential past 2030—a mortgage file, a trust account, the systems adjacent to them—is already exposed.
insights.locator: It is worth being honest about what can and cannot be recovered

insights.claim: Decrypted payment flows would reveal the structure of the US economy—supplier relationships to defense primes, defense contractor financing and sanctions evasion routes—making PQC an economic security and intelligence problem, not just compliance.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: National-security framing broadens political support and funding for financial-sector PQC.
insights.locator: The program is expensive and invisible

insights.claim: Post-quantum migration is a multiyear engineering program—cryptographic inventory, crypto-agility, then replacing protocols, certificates, hardware security modules and third-party interfaces—and most institutions do not know where their keys live.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Demand for cryptographic discovery and crypto-agility tooling is structural.
insights.locator: Mitigation begins with a cryptographic inventory

insights.claim: Of roughly 400 SEC-reporting depository institutions (out of ~8,500 federally insured: ~4,280 banks/thrifts and ~4,250 credit unions), only about 1 in 10 mentioned quantum in annual filings over the past year, usually as a single line.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Disclosure gap means investors cannot assess bank PQC risk; mandated disclosure could come.
insights.locator: Is the United States Ready for Post-Quantum Migration?

insights.claim: Disclosure is disconnected from action: Wells Fargo collaborates on NIST's post-quantum migration project yet its annual report never says 'quantum'; Ally Financial describes a multiyear PQC program only in its proxy; Banco Santander claims PQC leadership globally.
insights.speaker: CSIS
entities: National Institute of Standards and Technology
insights.so_what: Look beyond 10-Ks (proxies, NIST collaborations) to gauge bank PQC readiness.
insights.locator: What institutions disclose bears no relationship

insights.claim: Swiss supervisors found 72% of 60 surveyed financial institutions had not planned or implemented quantum-safe encryption measures, and Hong Kong announced a Quantum Preparedness Index, while no US supervisor has measured quantum readiness.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Global banking sector is broadly unprepared; large addressable market for PQC migration services.
insights.locator: Other governments have measured quantum readiness

insights.claim: A BIS Innovation Hub pilot with the Bank of Italy, Bank of France, Deutsche Bundesbank, Nexi-Colt and SWIFT found post-quantum signature verification averaged 209.9 ms versus 28.1 ms for traditional cryptography, with larger keys and more infrastructure, though all tests succeeded.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: ~7x latency hit implies hardware and infrastructure upgrades for payment systems.

insights.claim: Most smaller banks' cryptography is embedded in core processors like FIS, Fiserv and Jack Henry, none of which has published a comprehensive post-quantum migration timetable; Jack Henry's 2026 top cybersecurity trends list omits quantum.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Core processors face likely supervisory scrutiny and PQC migration costs; also a potential upsell opportunity.
insights.locator: Shared infrastructure and the concentration of technology vendors

insights.claim: Because shared vendor infrastructure can be fixed once and inherited many times, 8,500 separate remediation programs largely collapse into a small set of vendor migrations that regulators can examine directly under the Bank Service Company Act.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Vendor exams would concentrate PQC workload and spending at a few core processors.
insights.locator: Examine the vendors, not only the banks

insights.claim: Y2K succeeded because of a date certain, examination against that date and shared vendor infrastructure; by Q1 1999, 95% of national banks had completed testing against the FFIEC's December 31, 1998 milestone. PQC migration has only the third condition.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Expect a Y2K-like spending surge once a supervisory date is set.

insights.claim: Treasury and the FFIEC should align bank post-quantum exam expectations to the federal 2030-2031 gates, FSOC should label delayed migration a systemic vulnerability and publish a readiness measure, and Congress should push via hearings and the National Quantum Initiative Act reauthorization.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: An FSOC designation would be a clear catalyst for bank cybersecurity budgets and PQC vendors.
insights.quote: a migration plan without a required completion date is not a plan
insights.locator: Four Steps to Prepare U.S. Banking
